newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: China curbs diesel imports by foreign-funded firms.
newsitem.headline: China curbs diesel imports by foreign-funded firms.

text.p: Diesel imports into China's special economic zones have dropped significantly after Beijing curbed imports by foreign-joint ventures, Chinese sources and traders said on Tuesday.

"Diesel imports in coastal economic zones have been dropping. It's no longer easy to bring in diesel through this channel," said a trader with China National United Oil Corp (China Oil), one of China's state oil importers.
China has operated a crack down on oil product smuggling all year. Its latest move involves targeting firms with foreign shareholders which are allowed to import diesel, Chinese sources said.
China allows foreign-invested firms in five special economic zones -- Shenzhen, Xiamen, Shantou, Zhuhai and Hainan -- to import low-tariff diesel for their own use.
By the end of 1996, there were 39,504 foreign-invested firms in the five zones, a State Council official said.
But the government says many of the foreign-invested companies sold the diesel into domestic markets for a profit, abusing the privilages offered by the government, Chinese officials said.
Selling on imports became lucrative because the price of imported diesel fell below domestic prices in many areas.

A source with China National Chemicals Import and Export Corp (SINOCHEM), another state importer, said diesel import curbs on foreign-invested companies started in late June and were likely to last through the second half of the year.

"We've received various reports from the State Council repeating that current diesel stocks must be consumed first, which means companies in economic zones must buy from domestic refineries, instead of importing themselves," the source said.

"It's not (that) they can not import but they must have very good reasons," said the source, adding that authorities would even trace the diesel after granting approval to ensure the oil did not flow into domestic markets.
Figures for diesel imports by foreign-invested firms were not available but several Chinese sources noted such imports have dropped "in large scales."
"It has been very difficult for economic zones to get approval for diesel imports recently," said a source with China International United Petroleum and Chemicals Co (UNIPEC).
The source said China's processing crude imports could slow down in the second half if Chinese refineries cut down their diesel production in the face of high stocks.
"So far our crude imports are still normal, but the high diesel stocks are a big concern," the UNIPEC source said.

Amid high diesel stocks since early 1997, China has stopped issuing fresh diesel import licences for the third quarter and traders said the cut back could last throughout the year unless diesel stocks fall.
Chinese traders said it would take two months to absorb China's current diesel stocks if no new imports were allowed.
China imported huge amount of diesel late 1996 after using up its own diesel stocks when international diesel prices hit five-year highs.
Strong imports continued into the first half of 1997 and rampant smuggling as well as a state policy to encourage more diesel production further piled up diesel stocks at refineries.
"Diesel sold from economic zones is another reason diesel stocks are so high. It seems this time the government is determined to take action," the SINOCHEM source said.
-- Singapore Newsroom (65 870 3571)
